newsitem.title: CHINA: China shrugs off new U.S. trade concerns.
newsitem.headline: China shrugs off new U.S. trade concerns.

text.p: China on Thursday shrugged off new concerns by the United States over trade and said its stance on the American deficit had not changed.
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said on Tuesday the United States was concerned that growth in its exports to China had slowed considerably after increasing earlier in the decade.
"The U.S. trade deficit with China is not a new issue," said a spokesman for China's Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation.

China in March issued a white paper on its trade position with the United States, saying it was concerned about the issue and was encouraging domestic companies to increase imports from the United States.
But Washington needed to relax limits on exports of technology to China and boost U.S. government export financing to help reduce the trade gap, Chinese officials have said.
"China's position has not changed," the spokesman said.
Barshefsky said U.S. exports to China had grown sharply between 1992 and 1995 but had slowed last year and a further slackening was apparent this year.
The yawning trade gap has played a large part in the debate over whether Washington should renew China's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trade status.
MFN gives imports from China the same duty treatment as goods purchased from most of America's trading partners.
President Clinton has decided to renew MFN but opponents are gathering their forces for a challenge in Congress.
Opponents of renewing MFN have said the U.S. trade deficit with China could rise to $50 billion in 1997. The United States put the deficit with China at close to $40 billion in 1996.
